speechtext:
However, despite the catcalls from one of our colleages on the other side of the House, permit me, at a time when a significant development has occurred in the country, to depart from the matter before us for just a moment to congratulate the first ministers of Canada who have today, apparently, with but one exception, come to an accord with respect to the Constitution of Canada reserving, of course, unto myself the right, after an examination of the proposed changes in the resolution now currently before this House, to determine whether those amendments indeed deserve the approval of all hon. members, including myself.
While this day, as I have indicated, may not be very significant to hon. members in measuring days of glory, I think it goes without saying that this bill does, however, touch many of the citizens of Canada with respect to an issue in connection with which they have expressed their views on numerous occasions, both to us individually and to the government generally, without appropriate response.
The bill itself in an uncomplicated fashion would add to Section 79(1) of the Public Service Staff Relations Act the words "convenience, mobility or economic wellbeing of the
Right to Strike
public", which would require, as a consequence of those additional words, the potential designation as designated employees who cannot strike in the public service, pursuant to the provisions of Section 101(1) of the act, employees who render services which, if withdrawn, would affect the convenience, mobility or economic wellbeing of Canadians. Those additional words follow the words "safety, security," which now alone may be relied upon to categorize a group of employees as being among a designated group of public servants which does not enjoy the right to strike.
As the House will know, this bill was drafted at a time when one of the major groups of employees covered by the act sought to be amended included employees of the Post Office, now the Canada Post Corporation. The Canada Post Corporation Act, by Royal Assent on April 23, 1981, and by proclamation on October 16, 1981, transferred out of the category of public servants covered under the Public Service Staff Relations Act some 43,000 public servants rendering service to the public in the postal field.
I might say that the majority of the concerns which have been expressed to me, motivating in large measure my action in this regard, arose as a consequence of the disruption of service in the Post Office. I might say that with respect to that matter, in a speech which I delivered in this House on April 9, 1981, which is to be found in the Hansard for that day, I specifically made reference to the omission in the Canada Post Corporation bill then before the House of a referencce to a prohibition against the right to strike, recognizing that in deleting this group of public servants from the provisions of the act that I sought to amend and the act I hope to amend today there would be a detrimental effect on the over-all objectives of the bill.
How did I come to deal with this matter in this fashion? It was as a consequence of recognizing an obligation which, I believe, all members have and all members, if they reflect upon it, should discharge for the benefit of their constituents. My obligation as a Member of Parliament is to reflect here the views of those who sent me here, and those views are very clear. They are unequivocal.
I had occasion when first elected to dispatch to my constituents a form of questionnaire covering a number of topics of concern which had been expressed to me at the time of the 1979 election campaign, and I accordingly responded to those concerns by canvassing my constituents. Among the questions I asked was the following: "Should federal civil servants in essential services be allowed to strike?" The response 1 received was overwhelmingly in favour of the prohibition of strikes in essential services.
The riding of York North consists of a number of communities located within three towns, and without exception, although I analysed the results that I obtained from each one of these communities, there was a preponderance of opinion in favour of prohibiting strikes, to the following extent: from the community of Gormley, 94.59 per cent; from Kleinburg, 94.12 per cent; from Maple, 83.33 per cent; from the town of Markham, 86.29 per cent; from Oak Ridges, 78.26 per cent;

November 5, 1981
Right to Strike
from Richmond Hill, 85.23 per cent; from Thornhill, 90.84 per cent; from Unionville, 91.23 per cent; from Woodbridge, 89.47 per cent; and from general areas which were not designated on the returns, 87.4 per cent in favour of the proposition of prohibiting strikes.
Those results were accumulated from 2,676 individual returns which were submitted to me, being householder returns, representing the views of households and, presumably, the views within each of those households of at least two of my constituents. The average response, then, in favour of the proposition before the House was 88.25 per cent.
However, these results are not unique. They are in fact small in terms of the preponderance of view which has been determined by other bodies undertaking similar surveys. For instance, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business conducted a similar survey in 1978 asking the question: "Are you for or against the right to strike in the public sector?" Ninety-five per cent were against the right to strike, 4 per cent were for the right to strike. Bearing in mind that this particular questionnaire was submitted to independent businessmen in Canada, one can well regard their position as being indicative of the business community view.
Hon. members will also note that the question they asked was not as limited as the question I asked. Their question was for the prohibition of the right to strike in all of the public service, not the right to strike in essential services or those services specifically referred to in the bill as those services which, if removed, would create inconvenience, immobility or the lack of economic wellbeing to Canadians, a category which, in my submission, covers a wide enough scope to cover prohibition in essential services in the public service.
The interesting comparison between the results of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and the results that I obtained can best be explained by the fact that my questionnaire was submitted to all of my constituents. The questionnaire submitted by the federation went to business exclusively but there is not much difference. Certainly when we are dealing with percentages of 95 per cent or 88 per cent, one can appreciate the fact that the general public, including members of public service unions, from whom I have received correspondence recognize that it is improper to withdraw essential services from the public. That withdrawal occurs by the withdrawal of essential services required by all Canadians. There is a general feeling from the correspondence I have received to indicate that even public servants recognize this responsibility and are prepared to accept the proposition, quite frankly for their own benefit in many cases, that it would be appropriate if the right to strike were removed.
On one occasion during the recent strike of CBC technicians I had one gentleman tell me that he was in fact one such employee who no longer had gainful employment. He urged me to do what I could to see that the same thing that happened to him on this occasion did not recur. He found that he was locked out because the CBC would not negotiate in a
fashion acceptable to his union. His preference was to work but he no longer could.
My files are replete with correspondence that I have received, some of which I would like to read into the record. I have a letter from a Mr. J. R. Haggerty, a copy of which was directed to me. The letter is addressed to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston). Without reciting it all, I will quote some of the pertinent phrases in his letter which is dated September 8, 1981. It reads:
It is my understanding that you are proposing to initiate actions with a view to eliminating the right to strike by members of the public service, or at least those sectors designated as essential services.
He then goes on to say:
I find it appalling that government employees can go on strike and cause inconvenience and even danger to innocent people, and I suggest that legislation be passed which would remove the right to strike, and make this fact known as a condition of employment.
Mr. Haggerty underlines the fact that he would prefer that this apply to all sectors of the public service, but in the event it would not, he indicates a number of categories of employees who should be covered by such prohibition. On the second page of his letter he concludes by saying:
To my mind, the recent postal strike is a national embarrassment and Mr. Ouellet's comments about the unwise dependency of commercial businesses on the mail service make me sick. I believe he also said that there was no point in making strikes illegal because employees would only disobey the law. My God, whatever happened to respect for the law, and enforcement of the law?
If I may, I shall deal with a specific reference he made in his letter. It is well recognized that federal public servants have security of tenure. I recently had occasion at a committee hearing to question the Commissioner of the Public Service Commission who indicated to me that even in the case where there was recognized incompetence and misbehaviour of federal employees it took a full 18 months before they could be dismissed.
There is a security of tenure in the public sector which does not exist in the private sector in Canada. That security of tenure, coupled with indexed pension plans, should be recognized as having a value to offset whatever risk is to be borne by the removal of the right to strike. In many cases, from the standpoint of individual employees, as I have already indicated, this withdrawal of the right to strike can in fact constitute a benefit. The proposed amendment, therefore, is not antilabour. It may be anti-labour bosses, but it is definitely pro-employee. What is more, it is pro-Canadian and pro-public.
When we are faced with a decision in this House as to whom we serve, there should be no doubt: we serve the public. We do not serve the public servants. The public servants serve the public. I submit that it is our duty to see that that service is rendered, that it persists, that it is there and available for Canadians when they desire it and when, as a consequence of paying taxes, they have the right to demand it.
The second letter from which I will quote is from a Mr. G. R. Turney of Unionville, Ontario. His letter opens with the question "Who is minding the shop?" I shall quote part of his letter. In talking about the postal clerks, he says:
November 5, 1981

It's not the fact that the clerks are on strike that is the problem to me and the company I work for, but that all those other civil servants have chosen to honour the clerks' picket lines. There's the Post Office, Air Traffic controllers, Airport fire and emergency staff, Canada Customs-to name a few.
Mr. Turney goes on to say:
You think I'm frustrated? You bet I am! It's difficult trying to conduct our regular business profitably these days without these extra costly disruptions, none of which I have any control over. But you people in Ottawa have control. At least that's where the authority is. This country has enough problems in today's marketplace and the world, without creating more of our own.
Mr. Turney concludes by saying:
All these civil servants aren't civil and they don't serve. They just sit back with their guaranteed indexed pensions (which I'm paying for as a taxpayer dammit) and hold the country up for ransom.
Let's get this country moving and moving forward. I don't know how, that's supposedly your job.
This letter was written to me and I read those paragraphs for the benefit of my colleagues in the House. We have an obligation to discharge our duty today. It is an obligation that I urge upon each member. I refer to an answer given in the House by the then postmaster general on July 2, 1981. When I raised the issue of the Canada Post Corporation having a provision prohibiting the right to strike, the minister replied:
Just to take away the right to strike of employees does not necessarily avoid strikes. Those who believe very strongly in certain points will not hesitate to use the means at their disposal to register their point, and that could probably be by illegal strikes.
In my submission, that induces disrespect for the law. That comment is irresponsible. Canadians are a law-abiding group of citizens who are prepared to accept the law as we pass it here. To suggest that we dare not pass laws because we fear that some will disobey them is irresponsible.
What about jurisdictions that have imposed legislation of this kind? We know Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland have legislation prohibiting municipal police forces from striking. They do not strike.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROHIBIT RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext: What about Halifax?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROHIBIT RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext:
Exactly. In Halifax, Nova Scotia, there is no such legislation covering municipal police forces. In 1981 we had the delightful spectacle of a police force strike in the city of Halifax. The issue of the RCMP is well covered by the legislation as it currently stands. But the matter before the House is that, while certainly it may not extend today to the post office, or what was at one time the post office, it does extend to those other federal services which are being withdrawn by way of sympathy strikes to which reference has been made in the correspondence I have read into the record. The passage of this bill would stop that kind of sympathetic strike.
I believe, and all members of this House should believe, that Canadians are law-abiding and will accept the law passed by Parliament. That is the basis upon which we exist. I urge the House to consider this matter seriously. I urge the House to discharge the responsibility imposed upon every individual member to speak for the constituent, the people of Canada.
Right to Strike

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROHIBIT RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext:
I am pleased to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, basically because it is appropriate that we should be discussing this important subject matter. I should like to start by indicating to the House the purpose of Bill C-251, which is to broaden the class of employees who could be designated so as to include all who perform essential services. That poses a difficult problem for many people, and I will address that issue in my remarks.
Let me respond first to the hon. member for York North (Mr. Gamble). I am not a lawyer and I know he is. I think he knows there are no laws controlling illegal strikes in Nova Scotia. The common law of Canada, Britain and the United States did not grant the right to strike to public servants, but the legislative authorities, parliaments and provincial legislatures, could pass special laws granting this right, and that is in fact what happened federally in 1967 when the House adopted the Public Service Staff Relations Act. The common law, of course, does not grant the privilege of striking, but legislative measures can be put into effect which give employees the right to withdraw their services.

Mr. Speaker, just what is a designated employee? Pursuant to Section 79 of the act-I will not read it because those who are interested are aware of this provision-he or she is an employee who acknowledges that a designated employee as defined in that section does not have the right to stop providing or withdraw his or her services. Designated employees have indeed been the subject of numerous studies, and I recall sitting on the Special Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service whose report dates back to 1976. Our report was a follow-up on the special report of Mr. Jacob Finkelman, former Chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board. I should like to quote from page 47:13 of that report concerning designated employees. I quote:
Both Mr. Finkelman, in his report, and the Treasury Board, in its representations to the committee, proposed that the definition of designated services should be extended.
That is indeed what the hon. member for York North (Mr. Gamble) is advocating.
I continue the quotation:
In some of the representations from organizations outside the public service, suggestions were made which would have broadened the definition to include "essential services". Your committee feels that the phrase "essential services" is too difficult to define and would lead to the inclusion of most public servants. In other words the right to strike would be granted to public servants only to be denied by another process. In balance, we conclude that some extension of designated services beyond safety or security is necessary, to ensure that "health" be included, and to add a new dimension that of protection of public property.
Mr. Speaker, there is no question at all of extending the definition to cover the convenience, the mobility or the economic wellbeing of the public. I am familiar with the arguments put forward by the hon. member, and like him, I often receive comments from people in my riding who would certainly agree with his argument that in order to solve this problem

Right to Strike
we should take away the right to strike. I do not think this type of simplistic approach could be justified today, and I should like to put forward some arguments, or at least take a few minutes to recall the historical background of this issue, and then proceed with some more specific comments on the question of withdrawing the right to strike.
Mr. Speaker, in 1967, as I said earlier, the Public Service Staff Relations Act was passed, providing a statutory framework for collective bargaining in the Public Service. In 1973, the government asked the chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board, Mr. Jacob Finkelman, to make a study of the situation on the basis of six years' experience, and to make any appropriate recommendations for improving implementation of the legislation. Mr. Finkelman tabled his report in March, 1974. An order of reference from the House and the Senate was tabled and carried, establishing the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, on which I was privileged to sit with several members of this House, in fact, the member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) who sits here in the House was also a member of this committee.
Mr. Speaker, with several colleagues we carefully considered a number of questions, and one of the hardest issues to resolve was that of the right to strike in essential services. The committee met 40 times, dozens of briefs were received and carefully read and considered. All interested parties representing both management and labour testified: the public sector, the private sector, the business community, experts on personnel relations in colleges and universities, experts on labour relations, and university professors. Almost all those appearing before the committee touched on the burning issue of the right to strike in the public service. By tabling his bill, the member for York North has given us another opportunity to discuss this controversial subject.
I disagree with the member for York North that we should take away the right to strike from public servants. The arguments he has put forward are very familiar, but I feel that the solution he is proposing is not only ineffective and unwise but it also fails to resolve the basic issue, that is, how to reconcile the interests of the employee with the employer's efficiency objectives while improving the employee's working conditions. That is the problem and that is what collective bargaining is all about.
In both the private and public sectors it is important to ensure that paid services are not interrupted, especially in the case of services that are paid for by the taxpayer. We all worry about the increasing number of work stoppages which have on occasion become a threat to the public interest, which explains why naturally many people are becoming very concerned about the right to strike in the public service. According to the hon. member, it is intolerable that public services should be interrupted, and he feels that the government is wrong to allow such interruptions by continuing to grant public servants the right to strike, whatever the circumstances may be.
The question once again is how to reconcile the interests of the employee who wants his working conditions to meet with the objectives of the employer, who has to provide effective and reliable service to the public. The right to strike is an issue which does not concern the Public Service of Canada alone. In various degrees and notwithstanding a few important exceptions, the great majority of public employees at the federal, provincial and municipal levels-and I could include the education system in which I spent 11 years and where I certainly witnessed some strikes-have the right to strike. Yet, all their services can be considered essential to the public. It is therefore fair to say that a great many workers representing a high proportion of the Canadian manpower provide services which are in the public interest and that these workers want to keep their right to interrupt their work to make a point about a contentious matter with their employer. This, Mr. Speaker, is the purpose of a strike, to inform the public that there is some disagreement between the management and the employees. I once questioned an expert in this field, and he told me: "In principle, this was supposed to last two or three days in the past, but strikes have become longer, and I understand that there are even strikes which last so long that they seriously affect several economic sectors in a country".
On the other hand, certain proponents of the withdrawal of the right to strike in the Public Service of Canada tend to forget the accomplishments of the parties involved since the act was passed in 1967. Except for a few union leaders who have somewhat tarnished the reputation of the other, more serious and constructive leaders, the great majority of public service unions recognized as negotiators deserve in my opinion the gratitude of the public and of the legislators. They have worked seriously and honestly. Mr. Speaker, our public service unions have solved many organizational and administrative problems. In general, they show great respect for our democratic traditions and have developed a serious and respectable administration. Most of the union leaders have obeyed the law and have tried to contain the elements which favoured non-compliance. For my part, I like to believe that we also have to consider who sits on the other side of the bargaining table, a group of men and women representing the employer who deserve our respect and our support. They have had to adjust and to change with the times, often to bear with bitter criticism from all sides and always to keep in mind that their responsibility was to protect the public interest.
And if we look at the figures compiled by Treasury Board, this objective has been met. Indeed, during the period between the introduction of the act in 1967 and August of 1981, 667 collective agreements were signed. Of these agreements, 420 were signed at the bargaining table, which means that 63 per cent of negotiations were settled amiably without disruption of services. Of these 667 agreements, 164 or 25 per cent were reached by arbitration, once again, without work stoppage; and 56 or 8 per cent were reached by conciliation, once more
November 5, 1981

without work stoppage. The most surprising figure is the following, Mr. Speaker: 27 collective agreements, or a low proportion of 4 per cent, were reached following a strike. It therefore cannot be suggested or asserted that federal public servants abuse of their democratic right to strike. On the contrary, only an insignificant proportion of agreements were reached in that way.
Therefore the problem does not stem from the right to strike, but rather from the number of illegal strikes, wildcat strikes, and so on. Indeed, there have been 171 such strikes since 1967, including those by postal workers, air traffic controllers, radio operators, labourers, nurses and so on. To withdraw the right to strike would mean only one thing, Mr. Speaker, an increase in the number of illegal strikes. This is the real problem, and this is what we must deal with if we really want to prevent work stoppage. Legislative provisions exist for that. The House is aware of them, namely Section 27 of the Public Service Employment Act. Mr. Speaker, might I recall that in 1978, during the illegal strike of the postal workers, the deputy head threatened to invoke Section 27, which reads, and I quote:
An employee who is absent from duty for a period of one week or more, otherwise than for reasons over which, in the opinion of the deputy head, the employee has no control or otherwise than as authorized or provided for by or under the authority of an act of Parliament, may by an appropriate instrument in writing to the commission be declared by the deputy head to have abandoned the position he occupied, and thereupon the employee ceases to be an employee.
In 1978, recourse to that section was threatened. The Public Service Commission never received, as stipulated in Section 27, a notice to that effect. Which means that in fact it gave results, in that the workers went back to work. The act, as the hon. member said, is there to be observed and we must comply with it. I fully agree with him. All we need is that its provisions be implemented more strictly than is being done at present. That should go a long way towards solving the problem without for all that depriving civil servants of the democratic right they have and do not abuse. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point our that barely 4 per cent are illegal strikes, and if I add the 27 conventions settled as a result of work stoppages to the 171 illegal strikes, that gives a total of 198 illegal strikes. So, denying them the right to strike would not solve the problem, at least not to my mind, and will change absolutely nothing and only aggravate the situation.
The problems of public sector employer-employee relations are complex, Mr. Speaker, and I agree that no simple allpurpose panacea has been found. The Conservative Party during the last election proposed some form of dispute settlement, a whole series of what I think were probably quite reasonable measures to solve this type of withdrawal from work. But would it have been very effective? I doubt it.
However, Mr. Speaker, I do know the direction in which we should go. It is one which maintains the right to strike and the
Right to Strike
right to lockouts, which we do not have in the public service, as a tool for both union and management in the process of negotiations. The real dilemma for us is to find the means to safeguard the interests of third parties, such as the public, during this process. And this problem is not peculiar just to public service strikes. Withdrawal of service by airline pilots, refinery workers and so on can inflict as much damage as do strikes by air traffic controllers or postal employees. It becomes a problem of ensuring that responsibility for their actions be exercised by those wielding power. Unfortunately, we shall have to continue to provide punitive measures for those cases where responsibility has not been shown.
Perhaps we need to broaden these to include not only the traditional punishments of fines and prison but also the possibility for legal action by injured third parties against one or both of the parties involved in collective bargaining. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude my remarks by calling the attention of this House to the Special Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations. My only regret is that, to my knowledge, its 72 or 73 recommendations have never been implemented. The government did not act on them, except on the first ones where the D'Avignon commission was asked to look into one of our recommendations, to study the Employment Act and the implementation of the merit principle. Mr. Speaker, that document includes a host of ideas, honest solutions that were considered in depth by members of this House and senators. In my view, they could restore a degree of confidence in the collective bargaining process. I agree with the hon. member that the law of the land should prevail. This was also the committee's opinion. I would like to conclude on the following quotation, Mr. Speaker:
-your committee has no doubt that where the welfare of the community as a whole is concerned, the right to strike is not sacred and its suspension is the responsibility of the government and Parliament or the appropriate legislature.
The continued protection of the national economic or social interest can be provided by statute at the cost of a total denial of some rights now available to persons providing services to the public; or it can be protected by granting a statutory right to strike and imposing on government and Parliament the responsibility of determining when a strike has so affected the public interest that the right must be suspended.
Your committee recognizes that the public interest can be adequately protected by government and Parliament determining when and where the public interest is adversely affected. When Parliament is dissolved, the governor-incouncil should be similarly empowered.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I would ask the government to perhaps take seriously the matter of the right to strike and to use that as a vehicle to bring back the whole question of employer-employee relations before this House, in order that we may discuss further those very important matters, and I thank the hon. member for bringing this forward today.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROHIBIT RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
listened to the hon. member for York-North (Mr. Gamble)

November 5, 1981
Right to Strike
explain what he is attempting to do with this proposal. The longer he spoke, the more I realized how little he knows about the real world of work and the relationship between workers and management. There are strikes and there are strikes. There are strikes by workers which bother the hon. member for York North a great deal. There are strikes by corporations which he with his background ignores completely.
We have laws in this country having to do with taxation and how certain corporations, and I refer to the oil corporations, shall be taxed. The scope of those laws has now been extended by agreement between the Liberal Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) and the Conservative Premier of Alberta. The so-called law-abiding citizens who run the oil companies in this country have said they do not like that law or agreement, they are not going to abide by it and are now moving their oil rigs from this country to the United States. I did not hear the hon. member for York North criticize them for ignoring those laws and policies reached between the Government of Canada and Alberta.
My friend the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) wants to say a few words. I will leave him a few minutes. Therefore, I will not put on record as I had intended the profit figures to show how well the oil companies have done and how lightly they have been taxed.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROHIBIT RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext: Go ahead.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROHIBIT RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext:
No. I like the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton. I know that this question is important to him and I want to allow him a few minutes. I will find another occasion to put those figures on the record.
I want to deal with some of the points raised by the hon. member for York North. He wants to restrict the right of certain groups of public servants to strike. He calls them essential workers. Nobody likes a strike, not those who are adversely affected because a service they are used to has been withdrawn, and particularly not those who go on strike. All workers who go on strike lose the pay they would have received had they continued to work. Very few unions have the financial resources to give much in the way of strike benefits while workers are on strike. Workers do not go on strike lightly.
The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) put on record the small percentage of workers who go on strike as compared to the overwhelming majority who voluntarily settle their differences with their employers. I will not repeat what he said. When workers go on strike, it is usually with good reason. Often the reason has to do with pay. The hon. member for York North should not be surprised that, at a time when the cost of living is increasing by 12 per cent or more a year and workers are offered 3, 4, 5 or 6 per cent increases which would cut their standard of living, workers will not accept that. Sometimes they go on strike because living conditions are bad or their job security is threatened.
The hon. member said that public servants are not laid off. Many will be laid off because of automation and mechanization. The Post Office is a good example of that threat. Automation of the Post Office may have been necessary. However, the Post Office Department and senior officials were
very reluctant to give the kinds of guarantees the workers were entitled to so that they would not be displaced from their work. The hon. member shakes his head. If he would look at some of the studies done by judges in recent years, he would see that in every case a great deal of the responsibility for the dissatisfaction of the postal workers was put on management. The hon. member ignores that.
The hon. member wants legislation prohibiting strikes by essential workers. He did not tell us who they are. Are they the postal workers, hospital workers, librarians, those who pick up the garbage? Unless we know who he means, it is difficult to reach a sensible conclusion as to what we should do.
I point out to the hon. member that for many years a number of countries have had the kind of legislation which he proposes. For years Australia and New Zealand were held up as glowing examples of good labour-management relations. They had very complicated and sophisticated laws and regulations.
When times were good, the economies were booming and workers were receiving what they felt was a fair share of the increased productivity, there were very few strikes. In recent years, however, despite the legislation, they have had strikes. As the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier said, when workers do not have the right to strike legally, they strike illegally.
Let us look at our neighbours to the south. Over the years we have been accustomed to blue collar workers going on strike, the workers in the automobile plants, the mines and the lumber mills. That still happens. However, if you look at what has been happening in the United States in recent years, what do you see? It is the white collar workers, the professional people, those who, if it had been suggested ten years ago that they belonged to a union, would have been horrified and offended, who are going on strike.
Look at the record in the United States. In many cities there the teachers are now on strike although state laws prohibit it. Policemen and firefighters have been on strike. I am not saying I approve of those strikes. I say we should look at the reasons why any group of workers would go on strike, and try to deal with their problems, complaints and demands in a reasonable and sympathetic way. We could then cut down strikes, but not in the way suggested by the hon. member for York North.
The hon. member for York North made another point in passing with which I want to take issue. He suggested that in many instances, the workers do not want to go on strike but they are somehow forced to or coerced by the union or labour bosses. Nothing could be further from the truth than that, Mr. Speaker. There is a strike in my province against International Nickel Corporation in Thompson. That strike has continued for several months. The union negotiating committee several days ago, after meeting with management and with representatives of the labour department, has reached a tentative settlement. I have not heard today or yesterday what has happened. The news media reported that the workers were not satisfied with that agreement and were likely to reject it, despite the fact that their so-called labour bosses had recommended the strike.
November 5, 1981

The same situation occurred at Inco in Sudbury and it went on for many months. The same situation occurred at Stelco in Hamilton, Mr. Speaker.
I am not passing judgment, nor is any other Member of Parliament passing judgment with regard to these strikes. The point is, Mr. Speaker, that workers go on strike when they feel they are not treated fairly.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROHIBIT RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext: The Tories do not understand democracy.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROHIBIT RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Beaches (Mr. Young) says that Tories do not understand democracy. I believe that is a fair characterization of the member for York North. Part of the democratic system we live in is that workers have the right to belong to unions, and if workers are members of unions, they have the right to negotiate with their employers. They have the right to decide that they have not been able to reach an agreement that is fair and, therefore, that they will proceed to arbitration, voluntary or binding, or they will proceed to strike. The employer has the right to lock workers out. This is part of the democratic system in which this country and most democratic countries operate. I wish the hon. member for York North would understand that.
I shall deal with one more point, Mr. Speaker. Does everything I have said today mean that I do not believe there can be or should be any restrictions on the right of workers to strike? No, it does not mean that, Mr. Speaker. What I suggest to the hon. member for York North is that the best way to maintain harmonious relations between workers and employers, whether they be public or private, is to grant them the right to strike.
Does that mean that a group of workers who are part of an essential service should be permitted to go on strike and stay off indefinitely, regardless of the harm it may cause to the community? No, it does not mean that, Mr. Speaker. We have many illustrations before us where the governments, be they Conservative, Liberal or NDP at the federal or provincial levels, have said with regard to a particular strike that is adversely affecting the community that enough is enough. As I have said, governments, be they Conservative, Liberal or NDP, on occasion, when a strike has continued for too long and was really hurting the whole community, have passed legislation requiring those particular workers to return to work.
This is not a simple solution, Mr. Speaker. The agreement does not satisfy all those people who wrote to the hon. member for York North and some people who wrote to me. However, Mr. Speaker, it is a system that works best and impinges the least on the rights of workers, as it impinges the least on anyone else.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROHIBIT RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the wonderful advantage about private members' hour is that it allows Members of Parliament to advance any proposition they desire. It allows members on either side of the House, from time to time, to disagree with a proposition that is being advanced.
Right to Strike

In the few moments that I have, I think it would be a good idea if I asked hon. members to recall what Mr. Finkelman said. At page 124 of the first volume of the Finkelman report he said:
To my mind, to outlaw strikes by public servants at this juncture would be counterproductive.
I agree with that. He went on:
We should go to great lengths to make the bargaining process work better. "The best way of resolving impasses is to prevent them from arising." Then, if an impasse is reached, every possible step should be taken to encourage resort to arbitration, a technique whose time appears to have come. To compel public servants at this stage to rely solely on arbitration would tend to mobilize opposition to its use and would make of it in their eyes an evil to be avoided rather than a measure that might be looked upon as enabling employees to gain an equitable recognition of their needs without resort to disruptive action.
What Mr. Finkelman was advocating was a bit of good sense and an approach that would require the government and Parliament to examine a number of things.
We as a party have suggested, as the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier said, the establishment of a kind of public interest dispute commission. There is some doubt about the validity of that, but that was the suggestion put forward.
We have also suggested that this House should address issues that are negotiable but not arbitrable, to drive as many people as possible to see the efficacy of a reasonable settlement of disputes. As the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier said, "The record is not bad. There are violent exceptions but it is not bad".
